title: F4 – External analysis II: Life cycles, strategic groups and Blue Ocean
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 3 „External analysis“ (Teil 2: Industry life cycle, Strategic groups, Nintendo-Fall, Blue Ocean Strategy)

blocks.text: Industries are structures that change: introduction, growth, shakeout, maturity, decline – and the Five Forces change with them.
Competition often happens at the level of strategic groups (firms with similar strategic characteristics) rather than the whole industry.
Blue Ocean Strategy (Kim & Mauborgne, INSEAD) proposes to escape competition by creating new market space through value innovation instead of fighting in the red ocean.
Introduction: low rivalry.
Growth: low rivalry, low buyer power, high supplier power.
Shakeout: high rivalry – weaker players exit.
Maturity: high buyer power, low threat of entry.
Decline: high rivalry.

Defining the industry: neither too broad nor too narrow; criteria are geography, product segment, position in the value chain (airlines: Asia/Europe/US; leisure/business/freight). Industries converge (FinTech, EdTech).
Set of organizations with similar strategic characteristics; competitive dynamics are more intense within groups (grocery retail: supermarkets, convenience stores, corner shops).
Two dimensions to define them:
children: Scope of activities: product range, geographical coverage, number of segments, distribution channels
Resource commitment: branding & marketing effort, vertical integration, quality, R&D / technological leadership, size

blocks.text: Why use them:
children: Competition: with whom do you actually compete, on which dimension?
Strategic opportunities: which space is unoccupied – a white space (opportunity) or a black hole (dead end)?
Mobility barriers: barriers to entry between groups – can a firm move from one group to another?

blocks.text: Red ocean: existing market space where competition is maximized (detergents). Blue ocean: new market space where competition is minimized.

Strategy canvas: critical success factors (CSFs) on the x-axis, perceived performance on the y-axis. The blue-ocean player keeps adequate performance (above the minimal level to survive) on the CSFs where rivals fight, and invests in new CSFs that customers value but nobody serves.
Four actions framework (ERRC):
children: Eliminate: which factors the industry takes for granted should be eliminated?
Reduce: which factors should be reduced well below the industry standard?
Raise: which factors should be raised well above the industry standard?
Create: which factors should be created that the industry has never offered?

blocks.text: CitizenM (“affordable luxury” hotels): eliminate restaurants; reduce room space and reception (ambassadors and machines); raise low-cost construction (container rooms); create a combination of 5* features (location, bed comfort) with 3* prices.
Six red-ocean traps (Kim & Mauborgne 2015):
children: Making existing customers happier → focus on noncustomers
Treating market creation as a niche strategy → market creation de-segments markets
Confusing technology innovation with market creation → value innovation
Equating creative destruction with market creation → new markets need not destroy existing ones
Equating market creation with differentiation → also lower costs and prices
Equating market creation with low cost → also differentiation

blocks.text: Reorientation of strategic thinking: from competitors to alternatives, from customers to noncustomers; assess value (what do customers need?), industry (is there room to capture value? – Five Forces), firm (which CSFs to serve adequately, which new sources of value to focus on).

Successes: NES (1983), Game Boy (1989), Super NES, DS (2004) and Wii (2006) – low technical standards, low learning costs, fun, broad market – Pokémon Go (2016) and Switch (2017, hybrid console + portable, non-game features eliminated).
Failures: N64 and GameCube, 3DS (3D screen of little value but costly), Wii U (technically obsolete versus smartphones and tablets) – each time Nintendo tried to compete on technology.
Lessons: escape competition rather than imitate; customers, not producers, determine value; technology is neither necessary nor sufficient – value innovation opens new markets.

Risk of failure: Apple Vision Pro (2024, USD 3,499) – heralded as a new era, became a niche (comfort, battery, thin app ecosystem, unclear use case). WeWork claimed a “tech” blue ocean, but the Five Forces of real estate stayed the same.
Organizations in an industry that share similar strategic characteristics (scope, resource commitment).
Barriers that prevent firms from moving from one strategic group to another.
Creating a leap in value for buyers while lowering costs, instead of competing on existing factors.
Chart of an industry's critical success factors and the performance level each player offers.
Eliminate – Reduce – Raise – Create: the four actions to redraw the value curve.

sections.heading: Further thinking: using F4 in the exam

blocks.text: Strategic group maps: choose two dimensions that really separate firms (e.g. price level vs. breadth of content), place the case firms and discuss mobility barriers and white spaces.
Blue Ocean questions: fill all four ERRC boxes with concrete case features and check the traps – is the idea valuable to noncustomers, and does it lower costs as well as add value?
